items.prompt: A stream contains unsorted integer IDs. For every new ID, the program must immediately report whether that ID has appeared earlier. Which state signal most directly supports the requirement?

options.text: Store only the most recently observed ID.
Sort the processed prefix again after every arrival.
Maintain a hash set of IDs already observed.

feedback.reason: The decisive signal is repeated equality membership against previously seen values, not an ordering requirement.

blocks.text: A seen set represents exactly the state needed by the query: whether each value has occurred before. Each arrival performs one membership test and then records the value. The reasoning transfers to duplicate detection and deduplication whenever presence alone is sufficient; it stops transferring when the output needs counts, positions, or grouped members.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_prefix: Repeated sorting can answer membership, but it performs unnecessary ordering work and does not exploit the immediate equality-lookup requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.last_only: The last ID represents only one prior value, so it cannot answer whether an arbitrary incoming ID appeared anywhere in the earlier stream.

items.prompt: While scanning numbers, the program must determine whether a prior number can combine with the current number to reach a fixed target. Which observation is the strongest signal for hash lookup?

options.text: The answer contains two values, regardless of their relationship.
The input consists of numbers rather than strings.
The prompt mentions one pass, even if no lookup key can be derived.
For current value x, the needed prior value is the directly computable key target - x.

feedback.reason: The computable complement converts a pair condition into one equality lookup against prior state.

blocks.text: The equation prior + current = target can be rearranged to prior = target - current. That derived key is the mechanism that makes a hash lookup useful during a scan. The signal transfers to other relations only when the current value determines a concrete key to search for; merely mentioning pairs or speed is not enough.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_values_exist: A two-value output does not by itself imply hashing; sorted two-pointer scans or other structures may be more appropriate depending on constraints.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.input_is_numeric: Hash lookup depends on equality-addressable state, not on the primitive type of the values.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.single_pass_requested: A one-pass request is useful only when the needed prior state can be defined; without a lookup key or invariant, it is not a complete strategy signal.

items.prompt: Which requirement is a direct signal that presence-only hash state is insufficient?

options.text: Report whether any duplicate exists.
Report how many times each value occurs.
Report whether a specified value has appeared.

feedback.reason: Exact multiplicity requires a value-to-count mapping; presence collapses all positive counts into the same state.

blocks.text: A set can distinguish zero occurrences from one-or-more occurrences, but it cannot distinguish one from five. The requirement therefore signals a frequency map rather than a seen set. This boundary also applies to multiset comparison and threshold counts; it does not apply to simple duplicate existence or membership.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_boolean: A boolean duplicate decision can be made from prior presence; exact multiplicity is not required.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.membership_query: Membership asks only whether a key exists, so a set can represent the needed state without a numeric payload.

items.prompt: A program must collect all strings that share the same normalized signature into the same output group. Which state shape does that requirement signal?

options.text: A hash set containing only the signatures that have appeared.
One integer containing the total number of processed strings.
A hash map from normalized signature to a bucket of original strings.

feedback.reason: Grouping requires a canonical equivalence key and a payload that accumulates every member of that equivalence class.

blocks.text: The normalized signature defines which inputs are equivalent, and the bucket stores the original members that must be returned. A set is sufficient only when the output asks whether a class exists. The same signal transfers to bucketing records by category, normalized attributes, or composite keys, provided the key exactly represents the intended equivalence relation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.signature_presence: Presence can report that a signature exists, but it discards the members required to construct each output group.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.global_count: A single count has neither the equivalence key nor the association between a key and its members.

items.prompt: A service repeatedly asks for the smallest stored value greater than a threshold. Which fact makes ordinary hash lookup an incomplete primary strategy?

options.text: The input guarantees that values are unique.
The service receives many queries.
The service may allocate additional memory.
The query needs an ordered successor, not just equality membership.

feedback.reason: Hash state addresses equality keys; a successor query requires order-aware state or an ordering step.

blocks.text: The decisive operation is not “is threshold present?” but “which stored value is the least value above threshold?” A plain hash set has no ordering relation to navigate. Hashing may still support auxiliary membership checks, but the primary structure must preserve order, such as a sorted array with binary search or an ordered tree.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.values_are_unique: Uniqueness does not supply the ordering relation needed to find the next greater value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.many_queries: Repeated queries justify preprocessing, but they do not determine whether equality hashing or an ordered structure answers the query.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.memory_available: Extra memory permits several structures; it does not make a hash table support successor queries.

items.prompt: Arrange the checks and actions in control-flow order for a one-pass pair-existence scan whose lookup state must represent only earlier elements.

elements.text: Derive the prior value required by the current element.
Check whether that required value is already in the prior-state table.
If the required prior value is present, return the valid pair outcome.
Otherwise, insert the current value into the prior-state table for later elements.

feedback.reason: The current value must not enter prior state until the lookup that decides whether an earlier partner exists.

blocks.text: At the start of an iteration for index i, the table must contain only values from indices smaller than i. The match and insertion steps are alternative branches: a successful lookup returns, while a failed lookup records the current value before the next iteration.

items: Rearrange the pair relation to derive the prior value required by the current element.
Query the table before changing it, while every stored occurrence is guaranteed to have a smaller index.
If the key is present, return the pair outcome using that earlier occurrence.
Otherwise, insert the current value so only later elements may use it.

blocks.title: Why insert first fails
blocks.text: For input [3] and target 6, inserting the current 3 before checking would let index 0 match itself. Check-before-insert rejects that invalid pair, while [3, 3] still succeeds when the second occurrence finds the first.

items.prompt: A scan of n values performs one hash membership check and at most one insertion per value. Under ordinary well-distributed hashing assumptions, classify the expected time and extra space.

feedback.reason: There are O(n) hash operations with expected O(1) cost each, and the state may retain O(n) distinct keys.

blocks.text: Let d be the number of distinct values retained, with d ≤ n. Each of the n iterations performs at most two expected-constant hash operations, so n · O(1) = O(n) expected time. The table stores d keys, hence O(d) extra space and O(n) in the worst input-size case.

items: Time O(1) ignores the n loop iterations; expected O(1) describes one hash operation, not the whole scan.
Time O(log n) is too small for a scan that may inspect every value, while O(n log n) would charge a logarithmic operation per value that ordinary hashing does not perform.
Time O(n²) is not the expected bound under the stated well-distributed-hash and resizing assumptions; collision-heavy worst cases require a separate guarantee statement.
Space O(1) or O(log n) cannot hold up to n distinct keys, and O(n²) overstates a table with at most one entry per distinct input value.

blocks.title: Guarantee boundary
blocks.text: O(n) time here is an expected or amortized statement under the prompt's hash assumptions, not a universal worst-case guarantee for every hash-table implementation and input.

constraints: Assume a conventional resizable hash table with well-distributed hashes.
Count the lookup state as extra space.

items.prompt: A pair-finding task must return the two original indices rather than only report that a pair exists. Which lookup-state signal follows from the output contract?

options.text: Store only whether each prior value exists.
Store each relevant prior value with an original index payload.
Store only whether the target value itself appears.

feedback.reason: The required output includes provenance, so the hash state must retain value-to-index information rather than presence alone.

blocks.text: State selection follows the information needed at the moment a match is found. A set can answer the existence question but loses the original position. A map from value to an appropriate index preserves enough provenance; if all valid pairs are required, the payload may need a list of indices instead of one index.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.value_presence: Presence can establish that a partner exists, but it cannot reconstruct which earlier position produced that partner.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_presence: The target is a relation parameter, not the provenance of the values that form the pair.

items.prompt: Which problem statement is the clearest signal for a presence-only hash set?

options.text: The system must answer many exact membership checks over unsorted identifiers, with order and multiplicity irrelevant.
The system must return all values in ascending order.
The system must find the smallest stored value greater than a threshold.
The system must answer dynamic range medians after frequent updates.

feedback.reason: Presence-only state matches exact membership and does not promise ordering, rank, or range statistics.

blocks.text: A set stores whether a key exists and under ordinary assumptions supports expected constant-time operations. Sorted output needs ordering state, nearest greater needs an ordered structure, and dynamic medians need richer rank maintenance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_output: A hash set does not guarantee ascending iteration order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.nearest_greater: Hash membership does not directly answer an order statistic.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.range_median_updates: Range and rank updates require more state than global presence.

items.prompt: A new task changes from “has any duplicate appeared?” to “how many times has each ID appeared so far?”. What state upgrade transfers?

options.text: Replace presence-only state with a frequency map keyed by ID and increment its count on each arrival.
Keep a set because presence implies the count for every key.
Sort the stream after every arrival because counts need ordered values.
Store only the latest ID because earlier occurrences are summarized by membership.

feedback.reason: The output now observes multiplicity, so the retained state must preserve counts rather than only existence.

blocks.text: A set remains sufficient for a boolean duplicate signal but cannot distinguish one occurrence from five. A map from ID to count updates online and supports the current prefix's frequency contract without sorting the stream.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.keep_set: Presence loses the number of occurrences.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_stream: Sorting is unnecessary for counting and incompatible with immediate prefix answers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.store_last_only: The last occurrence does not summarize multiplicity.

items.prompt: Which input pattern is a strong signal for a seen-set lookup?

options.text: For each item, ask whether the same key has appeared earlier.
Produce a complete sorted ordering of all values.
Answer interval sums with no key equality.
Compute height from parent-child links.

feedback.reason: A set is the minimal state for repeated membership questions.

blocks.text: Insert after checking when the distinction is whether a prior occurrence exists. Add counts or indices only when the output requires them.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.global_order: Ordering is a sorting or ordered-structure signal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.range_sum: Range aggregation needs prefix or window state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tree_height: Tree recursion or traversal models parent-child structure.

items.prompt: Which wording signals a complement lookup rather than a generic membership check?

options.text: Find an earlier value y such that a relation like x+y=T holds.
Return whether any value has occurred before, independent of x.
Return all values in sorted order.
Find a contiguous range satisfying a monotone window condition.

feedback.reason: An algebraic relation derives the key to look up from the current value.

blocks.text: For x+y=T, the derived lookup key is T-x. The state may be a set for existence or a map for counts and positions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any_seen: That asks only for membership, not a derived partner.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.contiguous_window: Window state depends on adjacency, not arbitrary prior-key equality.

items.prompt: What output wording signals that a hash lookup needs a map payload rather than a set?

options.text: Return the original index or record associated with a matching value.
Return only whether a value has appeared.
Return the number of distinct keys with no identity.
Return any matching boolean regardless of the matched record.

feedback.reason: A set answers presence but a returned identity requires a value-to-payload mapping.

blocks.text: Store the provenance field that the output asks for, such as earliest index, latest index, or a record reference. Do not add arbitrary payloads without a contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_no_only: Membership alone is sufficient for that simpler output.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.distinct_only: Distinct-key count does not require which occurrence matched.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.any_order: If any witness is accepted, a set may still suffice, but explicit identity output requires payload.

items.prompt: Which wording signals a frequency map instead of a seen set?

options.text: Report how many occurrences or how many matching pairs each value contributes.
Report only whether a value appeared at least once.
Return unique values in ascending order.
Check a single key with no repeated input processing.

feedback.reason: Multiplicity requires a numeric payload for each key.

blocks.text: A set collapses all positive frequencies to one membership bit. Use a map when the count itself affects the answer or future state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.appeared_once: That is a membership signal for a set.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_unique: Ordering adds a sorting concern beyond frequency lookup.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_lookup: One lookup does not establish a repeated-count state.
